paragraphs.text: I think my city should adopt a carbon price, and I want to defend this position.
When pollution is free, people and companies have no reason to stop it, but when they must pay for each ton of carbon, they start to look for cleaner ways.
In my home country I saw how cheap energy made everyone careless, so I believe a clear price can change the habit.
Some people in my class worry that the carbon price will hurt poor families the most, and this is a fair point.
But the city does not need to keep the money.
It can give the revenue back to residents, for example through a small dividend or lower bus fares, so the low income group is not punished.
This way the policy stays fair while still pushing big polluters to change.
Of course one city alone can not fix the climate problem.
Still, I think starting local is better than waiting for the whole world to agree, because waiting usually means nothing happens.
For these reasons, my city should put a price on carbon now and use the money in a careful and just way.

note: ESL graduate-student essay on adopting a city carbon price; all segments origin "typed" (no paste, no ai, no cited/uncited). Simpler clauses and slightly awkward phrasing ("can not", "the low income group", "I saw how cheap energy made everyone careless") while keeping a coherent argument: efficiency rationale, fairness rebuttal via revenue recycling, and a local-action-now conclusion. 6 sentences across 3 paragraphs, ~215 words. Concatenated segments form the finished essay with trailing spaces preserved.
